messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 72
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Network Engineer
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 36

She is seventy-two now, a network engineer who still works part-time from home, known among her colleagues for her patience with tangled systems and her ability to stay calm when everyone else is escalating. She says that before the trauma, calm came easily to her. She had always been the one who could focus on a problem, isolate the signal from the noise, and keep moving.

The event she returns to happened three years ago on an ordinary weekday afternoon. She had driven to a shopping center after logging off from work, planning to pick up printer ink and a few groceries before heading home to make dinner with her husband. She remembers small details with painful clarity: the dry cold in the air, a song playing faintly from a car nearby, the shopping list folded into her coat pocket. As she crossed the parking lot, she heard shouting. At first she thought it was an argument. Then she saw a man rush toward another person near the entrance. There was a flash of movement, a scream, people scattering. She froze long enough to understand that she was watching a brutal assault unfold only a short distance away.

She did not know either person. What she remembers most is the victim’s face and the helpless confusion of bystanders looking at one another as if someone else should know what to do. She called 911 with shaking hands and crouched behind a car, peering through the windows while trying to relay her location. She can still hear herself speaking too quickly, trying to sound coherent. The police and paramedics arrived fast, but in her memory they take forever. By then she is already aware of a thought that later becomes familiar: You were there and you did nothing. Intellectually she knows she called for help. Emotionally, that never feels like enough.

In the days afterward, she expects to be upset for a while and then recover. Instead, the scene keeps breaking into her mind while she is doing unrelated things: loading the dishwasher, reviewing a network outage ticket, waiting for coffee to brew. The image arrives whole, as if someone has opened a video feed she cannot shut down. At night she startles awake with her heart racing, certain for a moment that she has heard shouting outside her bedroom window. Her husband reaches for her and she jerks before she recognizes where she is. She feels embarrassed by that, then irritated with herself for being embarrassed.

She begins to avoid the shopping center entirely, then any large parking lot. If she has to go somewhere unfamiliar, she studies satellite images online beforehand, checking entrances and exits the way she once mapped server paths. Her husband notices that she asks more questions before they leave the house: Where are we parking? Will it be crowded? Can we go earlier? She tells him she just likes a plan, but privately she knows it is more than that. Her body feels watchful all the time, as if danger is now part of the environment in the way weather is.

Work, which had always steadied her, becomes strangely difficult. During virtual meetings, if two coworkers talk over each other or someone raises their voice in frustration, she loses the thread of the conversation. She finds herself scanning faces on the screen instead of listening, alert to agitation. When an urgent alert tone sounds from her laptop, she feels a jolt in her chest before she can remind herself it is only a system notification. She still solves problems well, but it costs more. After a few concentrated hours, she feels wrung out and brittle. She says she used to enjoy troubleshooting because it rewarded persistence; now she is less tolerant of uncertainty, wanting things resolved immediately so she can stop feeling on edge.

Her world narrows in quiet ways. She chooses delivery instead of errands. She sits in restaurants only if she can face the door. She no longer attends the community technology workshops she used to volunteer at, telling herself she is slowing down with age. Crowds make her skin prickle. Sudden movement in her peripheral vision can make her gasp. She hates that her husband has begun to glance at her before suggesting an outing, as though checking the weather inside her.

What troubles her nearly as much as the fear is the change in how she sees herself. She has spent a lifetime believing she is competent, practical, not easily overwhelmed. Now she mistrusts her own reactions. She feels guilty for suffering when she was not the one physically harmed. At the same time, she cannot shake the sense that the world has become fundamentally less predictable and less decent than she had allowed herself to believe. “It was like watching a system fail in real time,” she says once, trying to explain it in the language she knows best. “Only there was no backup, no rollback, no clean way to restore anything.”

In the present, she continues to function. She logs in for work, makes dinner, calls her sister, folds laundry with precise creases. From the outside, much of her life still looks intact. But she measures every day against the possibility of being caught off guard. She sleeps lightly. She watches people’s hands. She notices exits. Some part of her remains in that parking lot, waiting for the next sound to split the afternoon open.
